draft.title: The gift of the Nile
card: Most of Egypt is desert, with very little rain. The Nile River runs north through it, so life in ancient Egypt was packed along its banks.
Each year the Nile flooded. When the water went down, it left a layer of rich black soil along the banks.
Farmers planted crops such as wheat and barley in this soil. The river also gave water for drinking and watering fields, and was a route for travel by boat.
Good harvests fed many people. Towns grew beside the river, and the rulers who controlled this farmland gained wealth and power.
draft.remember: The Nile's flood made a desert land farmable, and Egypt's towns and power grew from it.

a.q: Why was the Nile's yearly flood so important to Egyptian farmers?
opts: It left rich black soil that crops grew well in
It washed away the desert sand from the fields
It brought rain that watered crops all year
It stopped enemies from crossing into Egypt
a.why: When the flood went down, it left rich black soil on the banks, which made farming possible in a desert land. The flood did not bring rain, and the card says nothing about it keeping out enemies.
a.clue: Think about what the water left behind when it went down.

b.q: Ancient Egypt had very little rain. Where did most Egyptians live and farm?
opts: Along the banks of the Nile
On the coast, away from the river
In the hills, away from the flood
b.why: The Nile was the main source of water and fertile soil in a dry land, so people settled along its banks. Desert land had too little water for farming, which is why few people lived there.
b.clue: Where could farmers find both water and rich soil?

a.best: It left rich black soil that crops grew well in

b.best: Along the banks of the Nile
